title: "R syntax"
---

```{r}
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(gapminder) # used
police <- read_csv("data/police_killings.csv")
library(readxl)
```

This page covers the basic aspects of R's syntax and some common symbols might see in R code. Common base R functions used for managing packaging and data are instead on the [Base R](base-r.qmd) page.

## What is R?

R is a programming language and environment specifically designed for data analysis. Computer code is used for working with and analysing data, which when run is passed to an R [interpreter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interpreter_(computing) to execute. Inside RStudio, the Console panel is running the R interpreter in an [interactive shell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Read%E2%80%93eval%E2%80%93print_loop). It runs in a 'read-eval-print' loop, which basically just means you can type code into it, which is then read, evaluated, and any output - or error messages - printed (i.e. displayed) on the screen. After it finishes running code passed to it, it waits for any further code being passed to it. Within RStudio, when you 'run' a code chunk, RStudio passes the code to R and copies any output underneath the code chunk. R also maintains an active 'environment' whilst it is running, which is a collection of all objects - such as data frames, variables, loaded packages - created by any code that was run so far.

### Coding and Programming

coding
:   translating ideas into written instructions that a computer can run as intended

programming
:   broader set of activities also encompassing the design, architecture, testing, and maintainance of software

Fear and trepiditation are usual responses to hearing the phrase "we will use a programming language for data management and analysis". Some of this fear seems to stem from notions of what 'programming' involves. However, across all the semester 1 courses on the programme, what is covered is very much 'coding' rather than 'programming'. What we are interested in is how to use R to carry out a specific sequence of steps using computer code.

To try and make the difference more concrete. Using R to carry out a specific sequence of steps - like loading in a specific dataset and analysing it - is coding. Using R to create a package which provides features others can use in various ways with different datasets - such as a package to create and work with datasets consisting of LinkdIn posts - is programming.

In Data Project 2, we move to what could broadly be called 'upper beginner' R code to work with more 'messy' data that remains solidly within the 'coding' category - where the main differences are the number of steps to consider and handle in the initial data management steps based on the data you are wanting to work with.

### Coding Syntax

Computer code can seem overly confusing and overwhelming at first, with a big initial hurdle is getting acquainted with the 'syntax' of the programming language you are using: the structures and rules for how code in a given programming language need to be written. For example, if we wrote `example` without quotation marks in a line of code, this would be read by R as referring to an object. If an example object has not already been created - such as with `example <- 5`, which assigns the value 5 to an object named example - running code such as `example + 2` will result in an "object not found error". Place that word in quotation marks though - `"example"` - and R now treats it as a string of text rather than an object. Where if you try to run `"example" + 2` you will instead get a "non-numeric argument to binary operator" error - which is basically just R saying it is not possible to add a number to a string of text.

The reason I start with examples and the errors you might run into with them is because running into errors is a common everyday experience of working with code. The most experienced researchers will still regularly encounter 'basic' syntax errors by forgetting to include a `,` in the right place or accidentally deleting the closing `)` for a function. As a beginner though repeatedly running into errors can misleadingly make you feel as if you are somehow failing. With code though it is far more important to learn how to understand and fix errors rather than trying to achieve the impossible of never running into any.

## Operators

An operator is any symbol or combination of symbols which form part of a programming language's syntax for specific operations, such as `<-`, `+`, and `$`.

### Arithmetic operators {#calculator}

The easiest to begin with code in R is simply using it as a calculator using 'arithmetic operators'.

Most of this works as expect, except for use of `*` for multiplication instead of `x`:

`+` adds.

```{r}
2 + 2
```

`-` subtracts.

```{r}
21 - 4
```

`*` multiplies.

```{r}
5 * 5
```

`/` divides.

```{r}
50 / 20
```

`^` is used for power - so `^2` squares a value.

```{r}
3 ^ 2
```

Note, most programming languages, R included, do not use `x` for multiplication. One reason for this is because `x` could also end up as a named object, `x <- 2` (see [objects and assignment](#objects) below).

### Assignment operators

In `R`, it is common (and practical) to store values or data as 'objects'. Once values are assigned to them, objects are then stored in your current R session. Assignments are made using `name <- value`, such as `a <- 5` or `b <- 'Glasgow'`.

There are three main assigment operators in R: `=`, `<-`, and `->`. You will most commonly see `<-`, which is the 'left assignment' operator, meaning the evluated value to the right of it will be assigned to an object on the left. `=` is a functional equivalent to it. However, within R 'style guides' `<-` is favoured for assigning values to objects and `=` only used inside functions, e.g. `a <- some_function(b = 2)`. `->` is the 'right assignment' operator and will likely not often see used and many 'style guides' for how to write R code advise against using it.

Take the following:

```{r}
#| eval: false

a <- 2
```

As `<-` is a left assignment operator the evaluated value of what is on the right of the operator is 'assigned' to the object on the left. 'Evaluated' simply means that if any code needs to be run as part of what is on the right, that is done first before the output from that code is assigned to the object on the left.

Take for example:

```{r}
a <- 2 + 2
```

So in the above R will first 'evaluate' `2 + 2` and then assign the value of that calculation to an object named `a`.

To get the value for a simple object like the `a` object created above we can simply run a line of code with just that object's name:

```{r}
a
```

Importantly, because the right-hand side is 'evaluated' first, we can do calculations like the following:

```{r}
a <- a + a
a
```

When the above code runs, to evaluate the right-hand side R first gets the current value for `a` which was '4'. So, `a + a` becomes `4 + 4` which is 8 and now that is evaluated it gets assigned back to `a`, meaning if we run `a` again we can see its new value is now 8.

However, what if we run code without an assignment operator?

Save we first created another object:

```{r}
b <- 5
```

Then ran a calculation:

```{r}
b + b + a
```

We receive the value 18 but without `OBJECT <- ` before it this value is not being stored anywhere. In some cases that may be perfectly fine, we may just have wanted the result and do not need it for later reuse. But if this was a value we wanted to store without having to repeatedly type `b + b + a` every time, we can assign it to a object:

```{r}
c <- b + b + a
```

In the same way as you assigned these simple values, you can store other types of objects, e.g. vectors and data frames, `dataframe_name <- read_csv("data/file_name.csv")`. This is useful because those objects will be ready in your session to do some computations.

#### Assignments and Code Order {#code-order}

Say `a` has been assigned the value 10 (`a <- 10`), as in the screenshots in this section. If you assign a different value to the same object, e.g. by running `a <- 5`, you will replace the old value with the new. So, instead of having `a` representing the value 10, you will have `5`.

![The same `a + 2` run in the Console before and after assigning a new value to `a`.](rstudio_lab1_order-1.png){fig-alt="RStudio's Console: a + 2 gives [1] 12; then a <- 5 is run; then a + 2 gives [1] 7."}

The code `a + 2` remains the same, but the result from running the code changes based on the value assigned to `a`. That may seem an obvious point to make, but a large proportion of unexpected results and errors arise from changing what is assigned to an object. If variables suddenly disappear or your graphs unexpectedly show different results when re-run, it is likely that you ran code that assigned a changed version of the data back to the object storing it.

As shown in section above, it is also possible to use an object in a calculation and assign the result of that calculation back to the object. For example, if `a` holds 10, `a <- a + 5` is equivalent to `a <- 10 + 5`. Whilst that can be perfectly valid to do, care needs to be taken as now `a` is `15`. What do you think would happen if you keep running the same `a <- a + 5` line of code?

![After running a code chunk containing `a <- a + 5` and `a` several times, `a` has reached 50.](rstudio_lab1_order-2.png){fig-alt="An R Markdown code chunk containing a <- a + 5 and a, with output [1] 50 under it. The Environment pane shows a as 50 and c as 3."}

If you accidentally ran a code chunk multiple times which has such a compounding effect, the fix is to simply run your code again from the top-down (see [running your code again from the top](learning-to-code.qmd#from-the-top)). Thankfully, RStudio makes this easy to do in an R Markdown file (see [running code chunks](code-chunks.qmd#run-above)).

#### Functions return new objects {#assign-back}

Most functions in R for data analysis do not directly change the object - such as a data frame - passed to it. Instead, the functions return a new object with the changes. An explicit assignment back to the original object is required if you want to change it. For example, say we had a survey dataset we had read in and stored in a dataframe named `survey_data` and it had a column `ethnicity` for the respondent's self-reported ethncity. In many situations the data will be read in as 'character' data - treating each value as a string of text - rather than categorical. We can fix that by using the `factor()` function.

However, if we wrote the following:

```{r}
#| eval: false

factor(survey_data$ethnicity)
```

R will return output showing all the levels and values for a factor object created - but it is not actually being stored anywhere. This can be confusing as R displayed the values. However, that is R's default behaviour if code returns an output but is not assigned to an object. Compare running `2 + 2` and `a <- 2 + 2`. R assumes if you are not assigning the values somewhere that you are instead asking to view the values.

So, if we want to actually update our column we need to assign the output of the function back to our column:

```{r}
#| eval: false

survey_data$ethnicity <- factor(survey_data$ethnicity)
```

What the code is effectively instructing R to do is "take the existing data in the ethncity column, create a new object by converting its values into a factor, then replace the column with this new factor variable" (`factor()` is covered on the [Base R](base-r.qmd#factor) page, and the `$` [further down this page](#dollar).)

The aspect to be careful with is that when you assign the result to an object named the same as an existing object, you replace the *old* object. That is what you want when updating a column's type, but not when creating a new column. In that case, you would want to assign it to a different name:

```{r}
#| eval: false

survey_data$new_column <- some_function(survey_data$existing_column)
```

An example might be if had a survey where respondents gave their exact age, but for the analysis you are doing you wanted to also create a new column placing respondents into different age bands.

### Other operators {#other-operators}

- Relational operators are used for comparing, e.g. `a > b` asked "is the value of `a` greater than the value of `b`" and will return `TRUE` or `FALSE`.
- Logical operators check two sets of values and again return `TRUE` or `FALSE`. `|` is the OR operator and returns `TRUE` is either value to the sides of it is `TRUE`, e.g. the sides of `1 > 2 | 4 > 2` would evaluate as `FALSE | TRUE`, whereby the `|` expression here would return `TRUE` as one side of it is `TRUE`.
- Other miscillaneous operators exist, such as `%in%` which is can be used to check if a value exists in a vector or column and again returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`.

These operators do not make much sense on their own, but they are essential when wanting to act on data based on specific rules or patterns. For example, say you wanted to create a subset of your data, keeping only rows for participants living in Scotland, then your code would include `country == "Scotland"` (see [`filter()`](tidyverse.qmd#filter) on the tidyverse page).

Each of these returns `TRUE` or `FALSE`:

```{r}
1 == 5
1 + 3 == 2 + 2
1 > 5
5 < 10
'this' == 'this'
'this' == 'that'
'this' != 'that'
!FALSE
```

- Since `=` is used already for normal assignments and within functions, `==` is used if wanting to compare whether the left and right hand side are the same.
- `>` asks whether the left side is greater than the right. `<`, `<=` (less than or equal to) and `>=` (greater than or equal to) work the same way.
- `!` is used as a NOT operator, so when combined with `=` to create `!=` is interpreted as "is not equal to". It can also be used on its own before a value or object, so `!FALSE` is interpreted as "not FALSE" returning `TRUE`.

Then `&` and `|` combine two conditions: and `%in%` checks a value exists in an object:

```{r}
5 > 1 & 5 < 10
5 > 10 | 5 < 10
TRUE & FALSE
TRUE & TRUE
TRUE | FALSE
FALSE | FALSE
```

- `&` asks whether **both** conditions are true. In pratice, you might use this if wanted to create a subset of data with participants who are Scottish **and** currently employed.
- `|` asks whether **either** condition is true. Again in practice, this could be used if wanted to create a subset of data with participants who are living in Glasgow **or** Edinburgh.

Another operator will see quite often is `%in%` which is used to check if a value is in a set of values:

```{r}
"Labour" %in% c("Conservative", "Labour")
"Greens" %in% c("Conservative", "Labour")
```

### `::` namespace operator {#namespace}

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| filename: "Template"

PACKAGE_NAME::FUNCTION_NAME()
```

`::` is the **namespace operator** for accessing an object (such as a function or dataset) from a package, in the format `package::object`.

If you load a package using the `library()` function, you can call objects from it directly as `object` without needing to include `package::` before it.

It is common to load packages rather than rely on `::`. However, you will stumble across it in places. For example, the setup code chunk in a new R Markdown file (`knitr::opts_chunk$set(...)`, see [the setup chunk](code-chunks.qmd#setup-chunk)). It is also useful when working with two packages that both have a function with the same name. For example, if two packages, `package_a` and `package_b`, had a function called `some_function()` that despite the same name did different things and you need both for the code you are writing, you can access them with: `package-a::some_function()` and `package-b::some_function()`.

GenAI for some reason in responses featuring R code is overly fond of using `::` instead of loading packages, which gives misleading impression that it is used all the time, whereas there are plenty of experienced researchers who would not be able to tell you what `::` does as they never need to use it.

### `$` component operator {#dollar}

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| filename: "Template"

OBJECT$COMPONENT
```

`$` is the **component operator** for accessing named elements within an object, in the format `object$component`. In data analysis it is often used to access a column (variable) from a data frame.

For example, if a data frame named `survey_data` has a column named `age`, we can access it with `survey_data$age`. Here it basically means, from the `survey_data` data frame select the `age` column/variable.

### `[ROWS, COLUMNS]` subsetting operator {#brackets}

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| filename: "Template"

DATA_FRAME[ROWS, COLUMNS]
```

`[]` is the **subsetting operator** and is used to extract elements from an object. For a data frame the basic format is `DATA_FRAME[ROWS, COLUMNS]`, with the rows before the comma and the columns after it. Leaving either `ROWS` or `COLUMNS` blank selects all of them, however if want all rows you stil need the comma before columns (e.g. `DATA_FRAME[, COLUMNS]`). `ROWS` and `COLUMNS` can each be one or more numbers: such as a range like `1:10`, `c(2, 4)` for the second and fourth rows/columns, or column names in quotes inside `c()`, `c("VARIABLE1", "VARIABLE2")`. For example, `surveydata[1:20, c("age", "city")]` would return a data frame with just the rows 1 to 20 and columns named "age" and "city".

When it comes to more complex selections, the tidyverse's `select()` and `filter()` functions can do the same job in easier way (see the [tidyverse](tidyverse.qmd) page).

### `#` Comments {#comments}

Inside R code, any text after a `#` is treated as a comment and will not be run as part of the code.

This is useful for recording the 'why' behind the code, so future-you (and others) can quickly read and understand it. For example:

```{r}
#| eval: false

# Coerce numeric
police$age <- as.numeric(police$age)
```

Putting a `#` in front of a line of code is also a quick way to 'comment it out', where it will no longer be run if running the file / code chunk it is in. This can be useful when figuring out potential reasons behind an error message, where can 'comment out' a copy of your original code so you do not lose it whilst making edits.

Though one note of caution: if working in an R Markdown file `#` is different in Markdown syntax and is explained on the [R Markdown](r-markdown.qmd#hash) page. You can still use `#` for code comments, but it just needs to be inside of a code chunk to work as expected.

### `|>` pipe operator {#pipe}

This operator is what is known in programming as 'syntactic sugar': syntax which helps make code easier to read and write without changing any functionality.

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| filename: "Template"

DATA_FRAME <- DATA_FRAME |>
  FUNCTION1(ARGUMENTS) |>
  FUNCTION2(ARGUMENTS) |>
  FUNCTION3(ARGUMENTS)
```

The pipe operator passes the result of one function (or an object, here `DATA_FRAME`) as the first argument to the next, left to right. `DATA_FRAME |> FUNCTION(ARGUMENTS)` is the same as `FUNCTION(DATA_FRAME, ARGUMENTS)`, where `ARGUMENTS` are any further arguments the function takes.

Pipes can also be 'chained' together - passing the result from one function to another. So from the lines above starting with `DATA_FRAME` would run `FUNCTION1`, `FUNCTION2` and `FUNCTION3` in turn, and assign the result back to `DATA_FRAME`. A chained 'pipeline' can have as many steps as you need.

Another wonderful thing about pipes is that they let us break complex code over multiple lines. To do so, add the pipe at the end of the line before each function, then start each new line with an indent followed by the function If you type `|>` at the end of a line and hit Enter, RStudio will add the spaces at the start of the new line for you. Similarly, at the start of a line, if you hit `tab` on your keyboard, RStudio should convert it into a 2 space indent for you.

Let's use it with an actual function -

The `sum()` function adds numbers together, here in the format `sum(x, y)`:

```{r}
#| eval: false

1 |> sum(1)
1 |> sum(1) |> sum(5)
```

Using a pipe for `1 |> sum(1)` is the equivalent of `sum(1, 1)`. So the pipe lets us 'unpack' the first argument in each function, whereby line 1 reads as 'take 1, then add it with 1' and line 2 'take 1, then add it with 1, then add it with 5'. So a pipe can be read aloud as "then".

This may seem as if it is overcomplicating things, but as the code becomes more complex the value of the pipe operator becomes clearer. The second line above, `1 |> sum(1) |> sum(5)`, would be written as `sum(sum(1, 1), 5)` without pipes. Going left to right, `1 |> sum(1)` would be `sum(1, 1)`, and then `sum(1, 1) |> sum(5)` would be `sum(sum(1, 1), 5)`. Pipes then help us avoid `foo(foo(foo(...), ...) ...)` monstrosities in our code.

(In coding examples, you will often see words like `foo`, `bar` and `baz` used as placeholder names when explaining how coding syntax works rather than using real functions, and `x`, `y`, and `z` as placeholder names for variables / arguments; see [functions and arguments](r-syntax.qmd#functions).)

Plenty of functions take more than two arguments. Imagine we had a data frame named `df` and we were updating it by using - in order - `foo`, `bar`, and `baz` functions that each take arguments `x`, `y`, and `z`. Without pipes our code would be:

```{r}
#| eval: false

df <- baz(bar(foo(df, y, z), y, z), y, z)
```

This is a tangled mess: we want the result from `foo` passed to `bar` and its result in turn passed to `baz`. This ordering though gets visually reversed when nesting each function within the other - we have to read it inside out for it to make sense.

With pipes, it instead becomes:

```{r}
#| eval: false

df <- df |>
  foo(y, z) |>
  bar(y, z) |>
  baz(y, z)
```

Now it is easy to read and the ordering of the functions matches how we could verbally describe what the code does: "we are updating a data frame called `df` by running the functions `foo`, `bar` and `baz` on it in turn".

In online resources, older code, and textbooks, you may come across another pipe, `%>%`. This pipe comes from the tidyverse. The tidyverse pipe came before the base R one, and due to its popularity an equivalent was added to base R. Whilst you will still see it in use, and it remains supported in the tidyverse, the tidyverse itself recommends people start using the base R `|>` pipe. For the uses on these pages they work the same:

```{r}
#| eval: false

1 %>% sum(1)
1 %>% sum(1) %>% sum(5)
```

As the base R pipe is relatively new, most of the code generative AI tools were trained on uses the older pipe, and they default to it unless told otherwise.

## Types of data {#data-types}

In quantitative analysis, we often distinguish two main types of variables:

1. **Numeric variables** have values that describe measurable or countable quantities.
   - **Continuous variables** have values that can fall anywhere within a range, such as time and speed.
   - **Discrete variables** have values that are whole numbers that count something, such as number of children in a household.
2. **Categorical variables** have values that describe distinct, mutually exclusive categories.
   - **Nominal variables** have categories without any order, such as country, name, political party, and gender.
   - **Ordinal variables** have categories with a meaningful order, such as education level or level of satisfaction.

In R, the most basic data building blocks are **atomic vectors**. There are six atomic *types*: `logical`, `integer`, `double`, `character`, `complex`, and `raw`. In relation to our two main types of variables, we use **numeric vectors** (`integer` or `double`) to store continuous and discrete values, and **factor vectors** (a `class` built on `integer` codes + `character` labels) to store nominal and ordinal categorical values. Two other vectors we commonly use are **character vectors**, for text, and **logical vectors**, for `TRUE` / `FALSE`.

### Numeric {#numeric}

`numeric`
:   real or decimal numbers, such as `42` or `5.1`.

If you want to enter numeric values, you simply input the raw number without quotation marks. A numeric vector is usually stored as a `double` internally by default. The difference between `integer` and `double` is based on how they are computationally stored. Base R and most R packages handle the difference behind the scenes, so the difference in how they are stored does not matter to us.

### Character {#character}

`character`
:   text in quotes, such as `"Glasgow"`. (`'42'` as it is in quotes would also be treated as character.)

When you want to input text (referred to as `character` values in R), you need quotation marks, `'text'` or `"text"`. Character vectors store text, such as unique respondent IDs ("A102", "C006") and free-text answers.

### Logical {#logical}

`logical`
:   `TRUE` or `FALSE`, written in capitals and without quotation marks.

Logical vectors store boolean `TRUE` / `FALSE` values, useful for filtering and conditions. They are also returned as values when using 'relational operators', such as `20 > 30` which returns `FALSE` as 20 is not greater than 30.

Relational operators can be used on entire data frame columns and used to create new columns. For example, the code below would check values in an existing `age` column and return `TRUE` is 18 or greater and `false` if less than 18, storing the values in a new `is_adult` column:

```{r}
#| eval: false

survey_data$is_adult <- survey_data$age >= 18
```

### Factors {#factors}

A factor is a class combining `integer` codes and a `levels` attribute (see [`levels()`](base-r.qmd#levels) on the Base R page) containing the human-readable `character` labels for those codes. Each stored integer points to a character label in `levels`, so `1` might correspond to `"Conservative"`, `2` might correspond to `"Labour"`, and so on. For ordered factors, used for ordinal variables, R also records an explicit order of the levels to enable comparisons and sorting by that order. For example, if recording medal winners, there is explicit order of the levels for gold, silver, and bronze.

(How to make a factor from a variable is under [`factor()`](base-r.qmd#factor) on the Base R page.)

### Checking the type: `class()` {#class}

`class`
:   an object's classification in R that informs how R handles it.

```{r}
class(42)
class('42')
class(TRUE)
class(gapminder$continent)
```

You can use the `class()` function to check what class an object or value is in R. A column of a data frame is checked the same way, `DATA_FRAME$VARIABLE`. In the code above, we are checking the class for the `continent` column of the [gapminder](https://cran.r-project.org/package=gapminder) data.

(The tidyverse has a wonderful function `glimpse()` that shows the type of every column in a data frame at once (see [`glimpse()`](tidyverse.qmd#glimpse) on the tidyverse page). Changing a variable from one type to another is under [changing a variable's type](base-r.qmd#coercing) on the Base R page, and [inside `mutate()`](tidyverse.qmd#coercion) on the tidyverse page.)

### Missing values: `NA` {#na}

Within R, values designated as 'missing values' are grouped together and labelled `NA`. Importantly, this stands for "Not available" - covering all 'missing' data, i.e. data this is entirely missing and values designated as representing missing values. A common mistake is to assume NA stands for 'non applicable', which is a much smaller category and not always treated as 'missing' data analysis, resulting in inaccurate interpretations.

Note, summary functions such as `mean()` and `sd()` return `NA` if a variable has any missing values, unless told to remove them with `na.rm = TRUE` (see [summary statistics](base-r-statistics.qmd#statistics)). `is.na()` checks whether a value is NA [(and `!is.na()` whether it is not, see [operators](#other-operators))

### Vectors and `c()` {#vectors}

A vector in R is simply a set of values that are all of the same 'class' (i.e. there are all integer values or all character values). To create one, we use the `c()` function - with the 'c' being short for 'combine'. For example:

```{r}
ages <- c(12, 34, 10, 100, 32, 16)
ages
```

`c()` combines the values given to it, separated by commas, into one vector, here assigned to `ages`. If we were instead working with text values each would need quotation marks, `cities <- c("Glasgow", "Edinburgh")`, especially as we could also have text values with `,` already - `names <- c("Smith, John", "Baker, Jack")` - where the quotation marks make clear (1) that the words represent text and not object names and (2) where each text string starts and ends.

We often need `c()` whenever two or more values are given to a single argument of a function, as `,` is used to separate arguments in a function. If we had `function(1, 2)`, R reads each number as a separate argument being given to the function, whereas `function(c(1, 2))` makes clear that 1 and 2 are being assigned to the same argument. For example, we use `c()` if wanting to install multiple packages at the same time: `install.packages(c("tidyverse", "vtable"))`.

(And vtable's `sumtable()` is good example of more complex function where need to use `c()`, see [vtable](vtable.qmd). In contrast, a lot of Tidyverse functions are designed to limit number of situations where you need to use `c()`.)

## Functions and arguments {#functions}

Function
:   a named reusable set of instructions that can take inputs (referred to as 'arguments' or 'parameters'), run the instructions on them, and return a result.

Argument
:   input provided to a function that tell the function what to use and how to behave.

A function's name is followed by brackets holding its arguments, separated by commas.

In practice, you often do not want to specify all arguments when using a function. You give the ones you need, and the rest keep their default values. Those you give can be given by position or by name, so these two lines do the same:

```{r}
round(49.61532, 1)
round(49.61532, digits = 1)
```

- By default, arguments are read in same order that they are listed in the function documentation (here the number to round, then the number of decimal places).
- Any argument written as `word = ...` is what is known as a 'named argument' (`digits = 1` here), and named arguments let you specify exactly which arguments you are using despite the order they appear in.

![The 'Usage' section of the help page for vtable's `sumtable()`: each argument is listed with its default value, such as `digits = 2`.](lab4_digits.png){fig-alt="RStudio's Help pane showing the help page for sumtable, with its usage listing arguments one per line, data, vars = NA, out = NA, and so on, with digits = 2 highlighted."}

### A simple function

For what we cover on the programme, you will not need to write your own functions, but functions will make a lot more sense if we go through creating a couple of simple 'toy' examples. Say we wanted to create a function which takes two numbers and writes a string of text of the sum of the two together, we could create it with the following code:

```{r}
add_numbers <- function(x, y) {
  paste0("The value of ", x, " plus ", y, " is: ", x + y)
}
```

Here:

- `add_numbers` is the name of the function we want to create
- `<- function(x, y)` declares we want to create a function that takes two arguments, we will name `x` and `y`. (Argument names - with a few exceptions - can be pretty much anything you want.)
- all the code between the `{}` curly braces is the reuseable instructions for the function we are creating, which to keep things simple for this first example we just have a single line of code
- `paste0()` is an existing function to combine text and output together. Here we use it to combine strings of text, the original values for the arguments, and the value of the two arguments added together.

So, let's test it:

```{r}
add_numbers(1, 2)
add_numbers(5, 5)
```

### Functions with multiple arguments

When reading help documentation you will usually see multiple arguments listed, such as:

```{r}
#| eval: false

discount_price(price, discount = 10, item = NA)
```

If this was a real function we can tell by this useage example in the documentation that:

- `price` is required because it has no default value
- `discount` if not specified is 10 by default
- `item` if not specified is `NA` by default

In other words, it would be OK to write:

- `discount_price(100)`, giving value for price only if want to use the defaults for discount and item.
- `discount_price(100, 20)`, giving values for price and discount but keeping `NA` as the item default.
- `discount_price(100, 20, "Book")`, giving values for all three arguments.

However, what if wanted to give values for price and item, but not discount? Writing `discount_price(100, "Book")` would return an error as the function would create it as the value we are giving for `discount` which needs to be a numeric value rather than a string. To get around this problem, we can specify our arguments using their name:

- `discount_price(100, item = "Book")`

As wee reminder, by default arguments given are matched to the order you'll see in the useage example in the help documentation. So, you only need to name an argument if you are not providing a value for one or more arguments that come before it.

### Function example

Let's then create a slightly more complex function, similar to the imagined `discount_price()` above but with a few additions to cover more of the R basics covered in other proceeding sections:

```{r}
item_receipt <- function(price, discount = 10, percentage = TRUE, item = NA, bonus_discount_items = c("Book", "Notebook"), bonus_discount = 9.99) {
  savings <- if (percentage) price * discount / 100 else discount

  qualify_bonus_discount <- item %in% bonus_discount_items

  if (qualify_bonus_discount) {
    savings <- savings + bonus_discount
  }

  total <- max(0, price - savings)

  discount_label <- if (percentage) paste0(discount, "%") else sprintf("£%.2f", discount)

  writeLines(c(
    "------ Receipt ------",
    sprintf("Item: %s", item),
    sprintf("Price: £%.2f", price),
    sprintf("Discount: %s", discount_label),
    if (qualify_bonus_discount) sprintf("Bonus discount: £%.2f", bonus_discount),
    sprintf("Total: £%.2f", total),
    "---------------------"
))
}
```

So our new function can take a few arguments now:

- `price` that takes a numeric value for the price of the item
- `discount` with numeric value for either the % discount or absolute value discount being applied, with `10` as the default
- `percentage` (`TRUE` | `FALSE`) for whether `discount` should be treated as a percentage or absolute value
- `item` for the item name, with `NA` as the default
- `bonus_discount_items` that takes a list of strings of items that have a bonus discount on them, with `"Book"` and `"Notebook"` the two defaults
- `bonus_discount` with numeric value of the bonus discount to be applied (unlike the regular `discount` for purposes of our example, we are going to assume the `bonus_discount` is always an absolute value rather than a percentage)

This time we are also creating more reusable instructions inside our function.

- We create a new object inside the function itself - `saving` - and check `if (percentage)`:
  - If `TRUE` then calculate `price * discount / 100`.
  - Else (i.e. `percentage` is `FALSE`) then saving is assigned the same value as discount.
- We check if the item is in a list of items that receive a bonus discount, and store the `TRUE` / `FALSE` value in `qualify_bonus_discount`.
- The `if (qualify_bonus_discount)` means "if the value for `qualify_bonus_discount` is `TRUE`", in which case we add our `bonus_discount` value to savings.
- We then get our `total` by taking `price` and subtracting `savings` using `max()` - which returns the highest value passed as arguments to it. In our case, we pass `0` and `price - savings` as arguments. So, if the value of `price - savings` is less than `0` because we are applying more in discounts than the original price, then the value for `total` will become `0` as `0` is the highest numer.
- A new `discount_label` is created, again checking `if (percentage)`:
  - If `TRUE` then we use `paste0(discount, "%")` to use the discount value with a `%` sign after it.
  - Else we use `sprintf("£%.2f", discount)`. `sprintf()` is a function that let's us format a value, in this case `£%.2f` means "show a `£` sign and then the value of the variable - in our case `discount` - with two decimal places.
- We then use `writeLines()` to create output in style of a paper receipt. If given a vector of values, `writeLines()` will write each on its own line in the output. So we can create a vector with `c()` with text / code we want to use for each line of our receipt.
  - An opening "--Receipt--"
  - `sprintf()` to add rows for item, price, discount, and toal with relevant formatting. We saw above that `%.2f` formats a value as a number with two decimal places. Here we also have two rows with `%s` which just means print the value as a regular string. (You can find list of formatting options and examples on `sprintf()`'s help page.)
  - We also include another `if ...` for a line that will only be included if `qualify_bonus_discount` is `TRUE`.
  - A closing "---" line.

(Note, whilst our function creates a few new objects such as `savings` and `discount_label`, you'll notice these do not get added to the objects listed in the Environment pane inside RStudio when using the function. Anything created inside a function as part of its internal instructions is kept to its local 'scope' rather than added to the global 'environment' - unless it contains explicit code to do otherwise. This avoids functions - which can include complex operations requiring creation of multiple objects - from filling up the main global environment with things we do not need.)

Let's give it a try:

```{r}
item_receipt(65, item = "Book", bonus_discount = 15)
# At that price, it must be an academic book!
```

And:

```{r}
item_receipt(150, item = "Microwave", percentage = FALSE)
```

Or:

```{r}
item_receipt(95677.66, item = "1 kg Gold Bar", discount = 100)
```

This is why code is so powerful. We wrote 18 lines of code to create the function, but we can now reuse all that the function does with different values using just a single line of code - demonstrating 'abstraction' and 'encapsulation':

- **Abstraction**, a function provides a simple interface despite the level of complexity of its internal operations.
- **Encapsulation**, a function brings together all the operations and instructions needed to achieve a specific task.

As a user you do not need to know the full complexity and every intricate detail of how a function works, just what it does and how to use it. As someone writing a function, it may be tough doing the initial work, but once it's written you can reuse it again and again in a very simple way.

The power of code also compounds: As can also see, our two toy example functions - `add_numbers()` and `item_receipt()` - within their own instructions are using other already existing functions like `max()` and `sprintf()`. Our 18 line `item_receipt()` function will in turn through the functions it uses rely on dozens if not hundreds of lines of code written by others. But we never need to see that code to take advantage of what each of those functions provide.

### Help pages {#help}

```{r}
#| eval: false
#| filename: "Run in Console"
#| class-source: new

help(FUNCTION_NAME)
help(PACKAGE_NAME)
?FUNCTION_NAME
?PACKAGE_NAME
```

- `help()` opens the help page for the package or function passed to it as an argument (such as `help(mean)` or `help(tidyverse)`).
- `?` is a shorter 'syntactic sugar' way of doing the same.

If you check out a function's help page, you will see it has a lot more arguments than you will usually need when using it. It also says what the function returns, and usually has some examples at the bottom, though for some functions you may need to scroll down a bit in the help page to find what you are looking for.

When using RStudio, the help page opens in RStudio's Help pane (see [RStudio](rstudio.qmd#help-pane)), and only for packages that are installed. For a function from a package that is not loaded, give the package as well, `help(sumtable, package = "vtable")`. Though if you had already run `library(vtable)`, you can simply write `help(sumtable)` or `?sumtable`.

The help pages that open are part of the official documentation pages for packages. Some of these in addition to the help pages for each function also contain further pages with other examples and information about the package, which are worth a quick skim to see all a package is capable of.

## Other

### Naming objects {#naming}

Object names in R are case sensitive. Whenever R says it cannot find something, double-check for typos and capitalisation: `survey_data`, `Survey_data`, and `Survey_Data` will all be treated as different objects due to the differences in capitalisation. Names cannot contain spaces or start with a number, but you can instead use `_` to join words (`survey_data`, `simd_glasgow`, `life_exp_2007`) when needed.

This combination of lowercase letters and `_` underscores is what is known as 'snake case' and the style preferred in most R style guides. An alternative is one called 'camel case' which uses capital letters instead of undersscores when joining words, where `survey_data` in snake case would be `surveyData` in camel case.

### New lines and indents {#layout}

R lets us split anything after a bracket, comma, or pipe onto a new line. With long functions, it is common to start a new line after the `(`, then add each element that is separated by a comma on a line of its own, then add a final line with the closing `)`, as with this download of the [Northern Ireland Life and Times Survey](https://www.ark.ac.uk/nilt/2012/) from 2012, as an SPSS file (see [`download.file()`](base-r.qmd#download)):

```{r}
#| eval: false

download.file(
  "https://www.ark.ac.uk/teaching/NILT2012GR.sav",
  "data/nilt2012.sav",
  mode = "wb"
)
```

Here, the code elements inbetween the opening `(` and closing `)` are indented with 2 spaces. Compared to some other programming languages, like Python, these identation spaces are not a hard requirement in R. In Python spaces are meaningful for how Python's interpreter reads the code so a lack of spaces indenting the code when needed would produce an error message. As R instead relies on `()` and similar to know which code belongs together, it won't produce any error messages if you do not include indentation spaces. However, most R 'style guides' advise on having spaces to indent code for the benefit of yourself and anyone else who will read it - as the indents make it much easier to visually parse code.

(There are also some nice tools like `styler` which can 'auto-format' your code for you, including splitting it across lines and fixing any indents so it is easer to read. If you `install.packages("styler")` it'll be added to RStudio as an 'addin' too. You can then click 'Addins' at the top row of RStudio and select one of the features styler adds like "Set style" or "Style active file". By default, styler follows the Tidyverse style guide and running "Style active file" (which can also run from the Console with `styler:::style_active_file()`) will go through all the code in your currently active R script or R Markdown file and edit it to match the set style.)

### The `>` and `+` prompts in the Console {#prompts}

The `>` at the start of the Console's last line is R's prompt field - in other words where you can manually type code to run. It's also a good indicator of when any code that takes a while to run is finished as it'll display on the last line again once any code has finished running.

If the prompt instead changes to a `+` R is assuming the code you sent is not finished yet, usually because a bracket or quotation mark was opened and never closed, so it is waiting for the rest of the code before running it. Either type the missing `)` or `"` and press {{< kbd Enter >}}, or press {{< kbd Esc >}} to cancel and get the `>` back, then fix the code and run it again.

You will also see `+` at the start of lines in the Console when you run code that is written over several lines, such as a long function or a pipeline sent from a code chunk. This is just R visually marking the code to make clear where a single line of code is needing to be visually displayed over several lines or is an actual new line of code.

You will also encounter `+` at the end of lines of code when using [ggplot](ggplot.qmd), but its use there is different to how it is used in the Console.

### `[1]` in code output {#output-index}

When running R code you will often see `[1]` or similar at the start of the output. This is a label R adds to printed results, where `[1]` just means "this line starts at item 1". If there were lots of items, the next line might start `[7]` or `[15]`.

For example:

```{r}
1:30
```

(`1:30` is a quick way of writing every whole number from 1 to 30, so R prints thirty items, and the number in square brackets at the start of each line says which item that line starts at.)

### Data frames and their columns {#data-frames}

`data frame`
:   an object in R that stores data in a two-dimensional table with rows (observations) and columns (variables). We load a file containing a data set into a data frame within R.

The tidyverse packages use a modern version of a data frame called a 'tibble' (see [tibbles](tidyverse.qmd#tibbles)). For simplicity, these pages call both data frames. Reading a file into a data frame is covered on the [Base R](base-r.qmd#reading-data) page.
